pair_convention.spot_explanation: SGD/JPY at 122.96204 means 1 SGD = 122.96204 JPY. Rising = SGD strengthening vs JPY; falling = JPY strengthening vs SGD. Both source dossiers are written in inverted conventions relative to this cross — USD/SGD lower means a stronger Singapore dollar, USD/JPY lower means a stronger yen — and every stance has been translated into pair direction rather than copied. Both dossiers are independently bullish their own currency, which is the structural reason this pair's signal is muted and why the bilateral work matters more here than in a pair where the two views conflict.

executive_summary: SGD/JPY trades at 122.96204 as of the price store's 3 September close, meaning one Singapore dollar buys 122.96 yen, and the pair's recent history splits cleanly in two: up 7.13% over twelve months, but down 1.45% over six, 1.10% over three and 0.16% over one, so the entire annual gain was made and then largely stalled. The dominant bilateral narrative is a pair whose carry support is being legislated away by the quote currency's own central bank while the base currency's institutional appreciation continues at a pace too slow to compensate — SORA at 1.4028% against a Bank of Japan target of 1.00% leaves just 40.3 basis points, and roughly 80–90% of an 18 September hike to 1.25% would cut that to about 15. Two bilateral differentials diverge sharply from what either standalone dossier says on its own: a growth gap of roughly 535 basis points (Singapore +5.9% year on year against Japan +0.55%) that neither dossier frames as a pair signal, and a sovereign-and-terms-of-trade differential in which Japan's terms of trade have fallen 9.8% in two quarters against under 1% for Singapore while the ten-year JGB touched 3.00% on a fiscal risk premium that carries no currency-positive content. The settled verdict is Bullish tactically at conviction 2 (net score +0.1228) and Neutral strategically at conviction 2 (+0.0416) — a directional tilt on breadth, not depth, since the heaviest factor in the framework points the other way. The caveat is unusually sharp and it is a pass-2 observation: on 2–3 September the pair fell 287 pips, deleting the entire August recovery, as the yen rallied more than 2% on intervention speculation and Bank of Japan repricing, so the tactical long is now an entry problem as much as a thesis problem. The pair sits 3.19% below its 52-week high, at the 69th percentile of its closing range, below all three daily moving averages, and — critically — has now printed both a lower high and a lower low since late July.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no pair-level PPP construction available for this cross, and the REER-relative proxy carried in both dossiers is a statement about the yen rather than about the Singapore dollar. On the BIS real broad measure the Singapore dollar sits at 114.28 for June 2026, second-highest in the eleven-currency set, while the yen sits at 65.3 — roughly the second percentile of its own floating-rate history and 30.4 points below the next-cheapest currency in the set, having fallen a further 8.73 points over the year. Mechanically that gap implies an SGD/JPY at real-effective parity near 71.8 against a spot of 122.96204, i.e. the Singapore dollar screens roughly 71% rich against the yen in real terms — the largest real-exchange-rate gap either dossier records against any peer. That number carries no timing information whatsoever: the yen has been the cheapest major currency in the world for three years and the misalignment has not been a signal at any point in the cycle. What it does provide is a magnitude constraint on the bull case: further Singapore dollar appreciation against the yen is appreciation against a currency whose official sector has already spent roughly JPY 27.1 trillion this calendar year buying it, with the US Treasury publicly committed to joining again, and whose undervaluation Washington now describes in those terms. The base currency's own valuation is unremarkable — 0.15% from its 30-month mean — so essentially all of the valuation content in this pair sits on the quote leg, and it is a bounded-upside argument rather than a mean-reversion trade.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime is a pair that keeps grinding higher between official-flow shocks and has now taken two of them in five weeks. From the 30 April session — high 125.47217, low 122.09527, close 123.0243, a 338-pip range on the largest single-day yen purchase in the Ministry of Finance series — the pair rebuilt steadily through May and June and climbed to its 52-week high of 127.01629 on 24 July. The 30 July session then printed a 382-pip range and closed at 124.50913, with 31 July at 122.78567 and a 3 August spike low of 121.28953, as the record JPY 15,399.3 billion August operation and the 31 July joint action with the US Treasury took hold. August was a near-uninterrupted recovery grind from 122.58874 to 125.83134 by 1 September. Then it unwound: 2 September closed at 124.87104 and 3 September at 122.96204, a two-session loss of 287 pips (-2.28%) that deleted the entire August rebuild, as the yen strengthened sharply on 3 September on a combination of renewed intervention speculation and rising Bank of Japan hike expectations.

bilateral_carry_analysis.breakeven_move: A long position can absorb only 49.6 pips of adverse spot movement over a full year before carry is erased — less than one average day and one fifth of the 3 September range alone
bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The bilateral carry in this pair is small, one-sided in the base currency's favour today, and about to be legislated away. Because Singapore has no policy interest rate — MAS operates on the slope, width and centre of the S$NEER band — the only honest bilateral differential is a money-market spread of SORA 1.4028% minus the Bank of Japan's 1.00% target = +40.3 basis points for a long SGD/JPY position, or 49.6 pips annualised, 4.1 pips a month, 0.19 pips a day. Against an ATR(14) of 63 pips, one full month of carry is 0.065 of a single average daily range, so four-week outcomes in this pair are effectively 100% directional. The carry-to-vol ratio cannot be computed on the framework's intended basis because the pair has no implied volatility at any tenor. The regime assessment is that carry is not working for this pair and never was — it is a growth-and-balance-sheet trade with a rounding error attached. Post-hike the arithmetic collapses further: at +15.3bp the position earns 18.8 pips a year, and if the Bank of Japan reaches at least 1.50% by end-March 2027 as 35 of 54 surveyed economists expect, the carry turns negative and the base currency becomes the funding leg in its own cross. Forward points are not quotable for this pair because SGD has no listed future on CME or Eurex and no SGD/JPY cross-currency basis is publicly quoted; the table presented is an indicative covered-interest-parity derivation from the money-market spread, explicitly labelled as an approximation of funding drag, not a dealer quote.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is a genuinely asymmetric policy pair: Singapore has no policy interest rate at all, because MAS operates on the slope, width and centre of the S$NEER band, so the only quotable bilateral differential is a money-market spread. On that basis the Singapore dollar earns SORA 1.4028 per cent against a Bank of Japan target of 1.00 per cent, a slim advantage of 40.3 basis points, and it is the yen leg that is moving. A 25 basis point hike to 1.25 per cent on 18 September is carried at roughly 80 to 90 per cent on OIS with a hawkish dissent already standing at that level, which would compress the bilateral money-market advantage to about 15 basis points inside the tactical window. The offsetting Singapore channel is mechanical rather than discretionary — an estimated band slope of about 1.25 per cent a year, roughly 10 basis points a month of trade-weighted appreciation, of which the yen is only one basket component — and there is no scheduled MAS event inside four weeks. At the ten-year point the differential already favours Japan: SGS at 2.42 per cent against a JGB at 2.943 per cent on matched 31 August closes, minus 52 basis points. Transmission is direct: the pair's remaining carry support is being legislated away by a central bank with three scheduled decisions in the window, against a base currency whose instrument cannot respond to the yen specifically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the direction of travel in the differential is unambiguous and it runs against the pair. Half of 36 surveyed economists now name 1.75 per cent as the Bank of Japan's terminal rate and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50 per cent by end-March 2027, which would take the yen's policy rate above Singapore's overnight money-market rate of 1.4028 per cent and flip the bilateral carry from plus 40 basis points to somewhere between minus 10 and minus 35 basis points without Singapore doing anything wrong. MAS cannot answer that in kind: its instrument is a trade-weighted appreciation path, and even a steepening to roughly 1.50 per cent a year delivers only 60 to 75 basis points of basket appreciation over six months, spread across a basket in which the yen is a minority weight. The dated anchors are the 30 October Outlook Report and the 18 December decision. Against that, the base dossier puts 55 per cent on an October MAS steepening versus a published analyst community nearer 35 to 40 per cent, so there is genuine unpriced upside on the Singapore leg too. The net remains negative because the yen leg has a larger absolute move available, three dated opportunities to deliver it, and a rate that can actually cross above the base currency's.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential is the widest clean bilateral gap in this analysis and it points one way. Singapore's Q2 GDP was revised to plus 5.9 per cent year on year with plus 1.4 per cent quarter on quarter, and the Ministry of Trade and Industry lifted its 2026 forecast from 2.0-4.0 per cent to 4.5-5.5 per cent on 11 August; Japan's Q2 was plus 0.3 per cent quarter on quarter and roughly plus 0.55 per cent year on year, with private consumption contributing nothing for the first time in eight quarters. That is a gap of roughly 535 basis points on the year-on-year comparison. Labour markets say the same thing at a smaller spread: unemployment 2.0 per cent against 2.4 per cent, with Singapore's the lowest reading in the eleven-currency set. The inflation differential, by contrast, nearly cancels and is the reason confidence is not higher — MAS core at 2.0 per cent and headline at 2.2 per cent against Japanese core at 1.8 per cent, core-core at 1.9 per cent and the Bank of Japan's own ex-special-factors measure at 2.3 per cent. Transmission matters here more than level: in Singapore an upside inflation surprise steepens the appreciation band and is directly currency-positive, while in Japan it accelerates a rate cycle that is also currency-positive, so the two inflation channels offset and the growth channel is left carrying the factor. The dated tactical asymmetry is that Japan's 17 September national CPI, with an energy-subsidy unwind the Board has already flagged, is the larger single surprise risk in the window, and it is a pair-negative one.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the growth differential stays wide in level but narrows in second derivative, which is why confidence falls three points while the stance holds. Singapore's export engine is decelerating fast beneath a spectacular headline: semiconductor output growth has gone from plus 37.0 per cent in May to plus 20.8 per cent in June to plus 8.0 per cent in July, and non-electronics non-oil domestic exports are already contracting at minus 2.3 per cent while pharmaceuticals fell 56.7 per cent, so the plus 24.2 per cent headline rests on three product lines. Japan meanwhile has a shunto at 5.01 per cent for a third consecutive year, real wages positive for six months, corporate inflation expectations of 2.7 per cent one year ahead, and a Board that has reframed its objective from lifting inflation to preventing an upward deviation — a convergence in the inflation dimension that removes part of the pair's fundamental advantage. What keeps the factor Bullish is that Singapore's level of activity remains far above Japan's potential growth of 0.5 to 1.0 per cent, that MAS has explicitly forecast the positive output gap to widen in 2026, and that the Japanese distribution of price rises is still narrow — weighted median 1.1 per cent, services 1.2 per cent. Transmission runs through relative policy urgency, and on that measure both are tightening; on relative real activity, only one economy is growing at 6 per cent.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: SGD/JPY is a moderate-beta risk pair rather than a pure carry proxy: the yen is the world's funding currency and its most reliable risk-off beneficiary, while the Singapore dollar is a regional haven whose beta to global equity runs through trade and electronics rather than through portfolio flight. The current tape is close to the most pair-supportive configuration available. VIX closed at 14.43 to 14.51 in late August, down more than six points on the month, US investment-grade spreads are 79 basis points and high yield 260 to 263 basis points near historic tights, the Straits Times Index set an all-time high above 5,774 and the Nikkei is up 58.4 per cent over twelve months. In that environment the yen's haven bid is dormant and its funding role is active, while the Singapore dollar's haven bid is also dormant but its trade beta is working — an asymmetry that favours the base currency. The transmission is the carry channel: leveraged funds rebuilt 23,972 contracts of yen short over three consecutive weeks precisely because low realised volatility against a positive differential rewards it. The reason confidence stops at 55 rather than higher is that the complacency is measurable and dated risk is live — US and Iranian forces exchanged fire on 30-31 August in a disrupted Strait of Hormuz — and a genuine regime break would hit the pair from both legs at once.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk channel becomes genuinely two-sided for this specific cross and the honest reading is Neutral. The modal path is continuation — VIX near 14, credit at historic tights, both equity markets compounding — which keeps the pair supported. The tail is asymmetric and pair-negative in a way that is unusual for a haven-versus-haven cross: in a genuine global risk-off the yen is bought as the funding currency unwinds, while the Singapore dollar's regional haven bid works against Asian peers rather than against the yen, and Singapore is the most trade-dependent large economy in the set with total merchandise trade running at plus 38.6 per cent year on year and Greater China taking 22.0 per cent of its goods exports. The dated calendar in the window is dense with exactly the sort of event that produces that outcome: the US-China tariff truce expiry on 10 November, Taiwan local elections on 28 November, the US funding cliff on 11 December, and an unresolved Hormuz situation. Both legs would be hurt in the real economy by a trade rupture, but only one of them appreciates when volatility spikes. With a high-probability pair-positive modal path against a lower-probability but sharper pair-negative tail, and only a 0.05 weight, Neutral is the correct output rather than a manufactured direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two legs of this pair are measured with radically different instruments, and combining them produces no tactical signal. On the yen side there is a full dataset: leveraged funds are net short 77,042 contracts as at the 25 August report, a deterioration of 9,071 on the week driven by fresh gross shorts, but that sits at roughly the 33rd percentile of its ten-year distribution with a z-score of minus 0.56 and is 38,358 contracts less short than the 30 June extreme, while asset managers covered 5,627 contracts and dealers are net long. On the Singapore side there is nothing: no CFTC line exists, no SGD options in any CME product family, no CVOL entry, no options on the SGX futures root and no published NDF positioning. The only usable base-currency proxy is the estimated S$NEER deviation of roughly 1.7 per cent above midpoint on 12 August against a stated expected range of 1.40 to 1.90 per cent, which implies the market is already leaning long the Singapore dollar with perhaps 30 basis points of trade-weighted headroom before MAS's stated readiness to curb excessive volatility bites. So the bilateral read is a short-yen position that is not crowded facing a long-Singapore-dollar position that is close to its institutional ceiling — muted in both directions. Confidence at 45 reflects that half the picture is an analyst model estimate whose publisher pages no longer return a body.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the flow asymmetry turns modestly against the pair, because the largest identifiable latent flow in either currency is Japanese yen buying that does not appear in any positioning series. Japanese life insurers' currency hedge ratios sit at historically low levels on both Daiwa's FY2026 survey of ten majors and a Bank of Japan Review, and Daiwa states the mechanism explicitly: raising them would prompt corresponding demand to purchase yen. Rising Japanese rates and a resumption of Fed cutting are precisely the conditions that make that normalisation a consequence of the base case rather than a shock. Add GPIF ending the June quarter with foreign equities at 25.33 per cent against a 25 per cent policy target, which mechanically implies multi-trillion-yen foreign-asset sales, and three consecutive weeks of resident foreign-bond selling. Against that, the Singapore side has real structural inflows — a current-account surplus of 16.7 per cent of GDP, reserves up SGD 33.8 billion year on year, and MAS's 19 August asset-management package with a proposed fund tax exemption from year of assessment 2027 — but these are persistent and slow rather than convex, and the S$NEER already sits in the upper half of its band. The absence of any leveraged SGD futures book also removes the momentum amplification that makes other crosses trend: the base leg grinds, while the quote leg can gap.

That combination mutes rather than amplifies the pair signal: the yen short is not crowded enough to squeeze and the Singapore dollar long has roughly 30 basis points of trade-weighted headroom before MAS's stated readiness to curb S$NEER volatility becomes relevant.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A 17 September Japanese core CPI print at or above 2.0 per cent followed by an 18 September hike delivered with explicit pace-acceleration language, against a Federal Reserve that holds on 16 September — the sequence that reprices the yen leg from both ends inside 48 hours with 143,570 gross yen shorts outstanding.
tactical.historical_analogue: The 31 July joint Japan-US intervention forced 41,165 contracts of yen covering in a single week; the pair's yen leg gave back more than half of that move within four weeks, which is the evidence that a positioning squeeze in this cross fades unless a rate repricing accompanies it.
tactical.contrarian_case: The contrarian case against a bullish pair stance is not a crowded long but an institutional ceiling: the base currency's own central bank has said it stands ready to curb excessive volatility in the S$NEER, while the quote currency's finance ministry has spent roughly JPY 27.1 trillion buying yen this year with the US Treasury publicly committed to joining again. Both official sectors lean against SGD/JPY upside and neither leans against downside, which is a genuinely unusual asymmetry for a cross and is why this factor is Neutral rather than Bullish.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Strategically the visible short in the quote currency is small while the invisible yen-buying option is large — insurer hedge ratios at record lows, GPIF above its foreign-equity target, three weeks of resident foreign-bond selling — against base-currency inflows that are persistent but slow and already priced into a band deviation in the upper half of its range.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A Bank of Japan terminal repriced above 1.75 per cent, or a Federal Reserve forced to cut early on a deteriorating labour market, either of which lowers Japanese hedging costs and converts hedge-ratio normalisation from an option into a flow.
strategic.historical_analogue: The August 2024 carry unwind moved the yen complex violently from a futures base that was more extreme than today's, which cuts both ways: it shows the mechanism, and it shows that today's 33rd-percentile short has room to build further before it fires.
strategic.contrarian_case: The contrarian case for the pair is that consensus is short the wrong currency: the yen's share of allocated global reserves fell 0.40 percentage points in a single quarter to 5.44 per cent, Japanese retail is net long foreign currency 2.05 to 1, and Japan has slipped to third-largest net creditor — every one of those is a structural short-yen position that must reverse if the differential compresses, and none of it appears in the CFTC data that makes positioning look benign. Set against a Singapore dollar with no measurable position at all, the strategic flow asymmetry is the clearest reason not to be long this cross for six months.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised +0.02 tactically and +0.01 strategically. Both legs are large net energy importers hit by the same Hormuz shock, but with an order-of-magnitude difference in exposure — Japan's terms of trade have fallen 9.8 per cent in two quarters against roughly 0.8 index points for Singapore — so the net commodity effect is an unusually clean bilateral driver for this specific cross rather than a background constant. Strategic kept to +0.01 because the factor is already second-heaviest by default and Singapore's export concentration is a real offsetting risk.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both economies import essentially all of their hydrocarbons, so the energy shock is not a differential in sign but in magnitude, and the magnitudes are not close. Japan's July trade balance was a deficit of JPY 638.3 billion against JPY 156.3 billion a year earlier, a 4.1-fold widening, with mineral fuels at JPY 2,680.4 billion or 22.1 per cent of all imports and up 53.5 per cent year on year on falling volumes; June produced Japan's first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months. Its terms-of-trade index has collapsed from 90.5 in Q1 to 81.62 in July. Singapore is also hurt — mineral fuels were its largest single product deficit at minus USD 24.7 billion in 2025 and its domestic supply price index is running at plus 33.4 per cent year on year — but its terms-of-trade index slipped only from 98.66 to 97.84, and it runs the largest current-account surplus in the set at 16.7 per cent of GDP against Japan's roughly 5 per cent, a surplus that is 27.6 times more primary income than goods on the Japanese side and therefore generates far less spot demand. The bilateral trade relationship itself is a mild offset: on IMF DOTS, Singapore exported USD 17.8 billion to Japan and imported USD 22.2 billion in 2024, a net goods deficit of USD 4.5 billion for the base currency. Transmission over four weeks is through the monthly data prints, which are the direct measure of who is transferring more income abroad.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.17 weight this becomes the heaviest positive contributor and the differential is structural rather than cyclical. Singapore's surplus of 16.7 per cent of GDP is absorbed partly through reserve accumulation — official reserves up SGD 33.8 billion year on year to SGD 549.3 billion — and partly through the persistent real appreciation that the S$NEER band institutionalises. Japan's surplus is larger in absolute terms but its composition has degraded: a record first-half current account of JPY 17.43 trillion in which primary income is 27.6 times the goods surplus, while the goods account has turned to deficit and the net international investment position actually fell to JPY 560.1 trillion by end-March even as gross assets rose, leaving Japan third-largest net creditor behind Germany and China. Investment income is a stock return that is substantially reinvested offshore; a goods surplus generates spot demand, and Japan's has gone. The commodity netting reinforces it in the same direction: with Brent between USD 90 and 93 and JKM LNG up 101.9 per cent year on year, the marginal LNG buyer is Japan, not Singapore. The bear case for the pair is Singapore's own concentration — three product lines carrying a plus 24.2 per cent export headline, 22.0 per cent of goods exports to Greater China and a 12.5 per cent US tariff on roughly SGD 9.5 billion — which is why confidence is 62 rather than higher.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish on both horizons with confidence rising from 55 to 62 as the weight rises from 0.08 to 0.17. Tactically the factor is expressed through two or three monthly prints and the terms-of-trade transfer is small in a four-week window; strategically the cumulative income transfer — roughly ten per cent of Japan's traded basket against roughly one per cent of Singapore's — compounds, and the composition of the two surpluses diverges further.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Singapore: net crude importer and refined-product and petrochemical exporter. Mineral fuels its largest single product deficit at minus USD 24.7 billion in 2025, with processed petroleum oils simultaneously its number-two export at USD 51.5 billion. Domestic supply price index plus 33.4 per cent year on year; terms of trade 97.84 in July from 98.66. Direction rule: oil up equals mild negative (single minus), partially recycled through refining and re-export margins.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Japan: imports essentially all of its oil and most of its gas with no meaningful export offset. Mineral fuels JPY 2,680.4 billion in July, 22.1 per cent of all imports and plus 53.5 per cent year on year, with crude value plus 87.8 per cent on volume plus 5.5 per cent and LNG value plus 22.5 per cent on volume minus 4.8 per cent. Terms of trade 81.62 from 90.5 in Q1. Direction rules: oil up equals strong negative (double minus); LNG/JKM up equals very strong negative.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the framework rules to this cross: oil up gives minus SGD and double-minus JPY, so the net effect is that the quote currency loses more and the PAIR RISES. LNG up gives double-minus JPY against a smaller Singapore exposure, again pair-positive. The magnitudes corroborate the signs: Japan's terms of trade have fallen 8.9 index points, or 9.8 per cent, in two quarters, while Singapore's fell 0.82 index points, under one per cent, over the same shock. There is a partial policy offset on both sides — Singapore's imported-cost impulse is what is forcing MAS to steepen the band, and Japan's is part of what is forcing the Bank of Japan to hike — but those offsets act in the same currency-positive direction on both legs and therefore substantially cancel, leaving the raw income-transfer differential as the dominant net term. That differential is roughly an order of magnitude in Singapore's favour.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair rises, modestly. Japan's fuel bill grows off a 22.1 per cent import share with no export offset and pushes a goods account already in deficit further negative, while Singapore's refining and petrochemical exports absorb part of the shock. The offsetting consideration is that higher crude raises the odds of both an October MAS steepening and a faster BoJ path, so the policy channels partly neutralise each other and the net move is smaller than the terms-of-trade gap alone implies.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair falls, modestly. Japan's terms of trade recover fastest precisely because its exposure is largest, its current account returns to surplus, and its goods deficit narrows. Singapore simultaneously loses the imported-inflation impulse that underpins the case for a further band steepening, so the base currency loses a policy support while the quote currency gains a real-income one.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: JKM LNG, then Brent. Japan is the marginal seaborne LNG buyer and JKM has doubled year on year, which is the single largest asymmetry between the two energy import bills; Brent matters to both but is more nearly netted by Singapore's refined-product exports.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This factor cancels, and the cancellation is the finding rather than an evasion. Both central banks have hawkish standing guidance and both are more hawkish than their published analyst consensus. MAS increased the appreciation slope at two consecutive reviews, in April and July, said the July move builds on April's, stated it stands ready to curb excessive volatility in the S$NEER, and its Managing Director said on 28 July that the April move placed policy in a favourable position heading into a stronger inflationary environment. The Bank of Japan's 10 August Summary of Opinions contains the formulation that the pace of policy rate hikes will be faster than market expectations and that it is necessary to accelerate the pace of adjustment, its July Outlook reframed the objective from lifting inflation to preventing an upward deviation, and Deputy Governor Himino called on 27 August for raising rates in a timely manner. Both therefore carry an unpriced hawkish tail: the base dossier reads the October MAS decision at 55 per cent against published calls near 35 to 40, and the quote dossier reads December Bank of Japan pricing at roughly 1.21 per cent against a Board saying the pace will be faster. Sequencing is the one asymmetry that does not cancel — the Bank of Japan meets on 18 September, inside the tactical window, while MAS has no scheduled communication in it — but that is a timing point already carried in Factor 1, so this factor is Neutral.

tactical.what_is_priced: Each market prices its own central bank as more finished than the central bank's own documents suggest, so both legs carry symmetric unpriced hawkishness and the guidance differential contains no exploitable four-week direction for the cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two guidance regimes remain hawkish, credible and offsetting, though for different reasons. MAS's credibility is structural: the band has run since 1981, the parameters are undisclosed so the market cannot arbitrage them, and the reaction function is now legible — it tightened in April before the shock showed in the data and again in July while the latest core print had eased. The Bank of Japan's credibility is empirical and improving: hikes delivered in December 2025 and June 2026, a hawkish dissent standing at 1.25 per cent, an upward revision to the FY2027 core CPI forecast, and the abolition of interim assessments of the bond-purchase plan, which raises the probability of unscheduled hawkish action. Where the two differ is verifiability and external pressure: MAS's slope and band deviation are analyst reconstructions whose publisher pages now return empty bodies, while the yen leg has an additional, genuinely unusual guidance channel in the form of a US Treasury publicly stating it expects Japanese policy to produce a stronger yen. That last point is a mild pair-negative and it is the reason this factor does not tilt positive despite the base currency's cleaner mechanism. On balance, two hawkish and credible central banks, both under-priced, net to nothing.

strategic.what_is_priced: Both guidance regimes are priced at a discount to their own documents, and the additional official pressure on the yen leg roughly offsets the base currency's more mechanical delivery, leaving no strategic guidance edge in the cross.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral on both horizons at identical confidence. The mechanism is the same at both: two hawkish central banks, each more hawkish than its own published consensus, cancel in a bilateral frame. The only difference is composition — tactically the Bank of Japan has the calendar and MAS is silent; strategically MAS gets a dated review while the yen leg acquires an Outlook Report and continued official US support — and neither difference is large enough to tilt the factor.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The dominant near-dated event risk in this cross is official flow, and it points one way. Japan bought roughly JPY 27.1 trillion of yen in calendar 2026, including JPY 15,399.3 billion between 30 July and 26 August and a joint operation with the US Treasury on 31 July, against a previous full-year record of JPY 15.32 trillion; the Finance Minister has said Japan will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention and the US Treasury Secretary repeated the commitment at the G20 on 31 August. There is therefore a well-capitalised, publicly committed and now bilateral official bid for the quote currency, and no official bid for the base currency at all — indeed MAS has stated it stands ready to curb excessive volatility in the S$NEER, which leans against base-currency strength rather than supporting it. Both official sectors are positioned against this pair rising, which is a rare and genuinely bilateral asymmetry. The second event set is the 16 to 18 September central bank cluster, where the FOMC and the Bank of Japan meet 48 hours apart with a Japanese CPI print between them, and the FOMC is the more ambiguous leg because a hawkish Fed lifts both USD legs of this cross unequally. Working against the bearish read is energy: Hormuz escalation hurts the quote currency's terms of trade far more than the base currency's, which is a pair-positive tail inside a pair-negative factor.

tactical.what_is_priced: The yen options market prices intervention risk explicitly and generously — a one-month 25-delta risk reversal of minus 1.74 volatility points against minus 0.32 for EUR/USD — but the cross itself has no options market in which that premium can be observed or faded, so the asymmetry sits unpriced in this pair specifically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the calendar fragments and the sign weakens, but it stays negative. The intervention option persists on the quote side with a demonstrated half-life of under a month, which limits how much weight it can carry; against it sits a dense trade-policy cluster that hits the base currency's real economy harder than the quote currency's. The US-China tariff truce expires on 10 November with China's reciprocal truce on 19 November and the exclusion process on 31 December, and Singapore sends 22.0 per cent of its goods exports to Greater China against Japan's 17.5 per cent, while Singapore is the most trade-dependent large economy in the set with total merchandise trade at plus 38.6 per cent year on year. Taiwan's local elections on 28 November are doubly acute for the base currency because its export boom is concentrated in integrated circuits and disk media. On the other side, the unresolved US tariff on Japanese motor vehicles — motor vehicles are 34.1 per cent of Japan's US-bound exports and the operative rate could not be established from a primary source — is a real quote-side exposure, and continued Hormuz escalation damages Japan's terms of trade more. The net is mildly negative because a trade rupture is a double hit to the pair: it damages Singapore's entrepot function and simultaneously produces the risk-off in which the yen is bought.

Tactically the risk is concentrated in a single, one-directional official-flow asymmetry with the September cluster attached, which is as clean as event risk gets in this pair. Strategically it fragments across trade-policy and election risk that damages the base economy while producing exactly the risk regime that supports the quote currency, offset by an energy tail that runs the other way — the same sign, less confidently held.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised +0.02 tactically and +0.03 strategically. This is normally a two-sentence differential, but it is currently the widest sovereign gap in the eleven-currency set AND acutely live on the quote side: the ten-year JGB touched 3.00 per cent on 1 September for the first time since 1996, the 25s30s spread is inverted, and an FY2027 budget request of about JPY 143trn with a JPY 36.6trn debt-service line lands inside the strategic window. That is an active repricing, not a background constant.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The sovereign differential between these two issuers is about as wide as the G10-adjacent universe offers and it is currently moving. Singapore is Aaa from Moody's and AAA from S&P, both stable, runs a projected FY2026 budget surplus of about SGD 8.5 billion or 1.0 per cent of GDP, and is a substantial net creditor whose gross debt of 171.3 per cent of GDP is issued under the Government Securities Act for investment rather than to fund deficits, backed by roughly USD 1.34 trillion of sovereign wealth against a GDP near USD 560 billion. Japan is A1, A-plus and A, with general government gross debt of roughly 214.5 per cent of GDP, an FY2027 ministry budget request of about JPY 143 trillion and a record debt-service line of JPY 36.6 trillion struck on an assumed rate raised from 3.0 to 3.8 per cent. The bond market is pricing that: the ten-year JGB touched 3.00 per cent on 1 September for the first time since September 1996, the two-year hit a 31-year high and the 25s30s spread is inverted at minus 1.0 basis point, which is a supply-and-buyer-base signature rather than a growth signal. The bilateral transmission is the important part and it inverts the naive reading: because a meaningful share of the recent JGB yield rise is fiscal risk premium rather than policy expectation, higher Japanese yields are currently pair-positive, not pair-negative.

tactical.what_is_priced: The JGB market has priced the fiscal deterioration and the FX market has not priced its consequence for this cross; the standard model reads rising Japanese yields as yen-positive, when a risk-premium-driven rise carries no currency-positive content at all.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months this factor strengthens because the arithmetic compounds and there is a dated event to crystallise it. Every further 100 basis points of Bank of Japan tightening adds roughly JPY 5 trillion, about 0.9 per cent of GDP, to the debt-service line, which means the quote currency's own tightening cycle is simultaneously a fiscal problem — and the Bank of Japan is stepping its JGB purchases down from JPY 2.5 trillion a month to JPY 2.3 trillion in Q4 and JPY 2.1 trillion in Q1 2027, so supply rises as the dominant buyer withdraws. The FY2027 draft budget approval in late December is the specific test, against a Prime Minister aiming to cap new issuance near JPY 40 trillion versus JPY 29.6 trillion in the FY2026 initial budget. Singapore, by contrast, has effectively unlimited fiscal space, is deploying some of it to defend a capital-inflow channel through the 19 August asset-management package, and has no rating watch, auction difficulty or debt-ceiling analogue. The offsets on the quote side are genuine and cap confidence: roughly 90 per cent of JGBs are domestically held, the Bank of Japan holds about half the outstanding stock, and all three major agencies remain on stable outlook with no 2026 action. But the direction of the differential is unambiguous, and the transmission to this cross — a fiscal risk premium that neutralises the yen's own rate advantage — is the single clearest structural argument the base currency has.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish on both horizons with confidence rising from 62 to 68 as the weight rises from 0.06 to 0.10. Tactically the factor is expressed through auctions and a budget headline that are partly discounted. Strategically it is the compounding arithmetic of a debt-service line that rises about JPY 5 trillion per 100 basis points against a central bank expected to add 50 to 75 basis points inside the window while cutting its own purchases, with the late-December FY2027 draft budget as the dated crystallising event.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Half of this factor's normal content does not exist for SGD/JPY and the other half is deliberately withheld from this pass. The direction payload states that implied volatility is permanently unavailable because SGD has no listed FX option on any exchange, which the base dossier independently confirms — no SGD options in any CME product family, no SGD CVOL index, no options on the SGX USD/SGD futures root — so implied volatility, the IV percentile, the variance risk premium, the term structure and the 25-delta risk reversal are all structurally null for this cross, not merely unfetched. The payload's funding block is likewise unavailable because no SGD future is listed on CME or Eurex, so no forward funding differential can be quoted and the policy differential must not be substituted for it. What can be stated is realised volatility from the cross tables: SGD/JPY has the lowest 20-day realised volatility of any yen cross at 3.92 per cent against a 60-day reading of 6.05 per cent, which is the signature of one managed leg dampening one free-floating leg. The store's own zone detection produced a marked asymmetry — only one resistance zone against ten support zones cleared the two-touch threshold across 4,879 weekday bars — which is a disclosed data-quality shortfall for pass two to supplement with round numbers, not a directional signal. With no volatility surface and levels withheld by design, Neutral is the only honest output.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the structural picture remains unusable in the same way and the weight falls to 0.03, so this factor should not and does not move the synthesis. The only strategically informative observations are structural rather than directional. First, the cross's realised volatility is materially lower than either leg's free-floating counterpart because the base currency is managed inside a band, which compresses the centre of the distribution while leaving the tails to be set by the yen leg — an asymmetry in shape, not in direction. Second, convexity cannot be bought on this pair at any tenor, whereas the yen leg alone has a rich and informative surface where the one-month 25-delta risk reversal is minus 1.74 volatility points and the one-year has decayed to minus 0.16; anyone wanting optionality on the yen half of this view has to buy it in USD/JPY, which introduces a dollar leg the cross does not have. Third, the store's zone shortfall of one resistance against ten support zones is disclosed here so that pass two supplements it with round numbers rather than presenting a lopsided level list as evidence. Confidence at 44 reflects a factor that is structurally informative about how to hold the view and completely uninformative about which way it goes.

expression_assessment.vol_landscape_summary: There is no volatility landscape for SGD/JPY. Implied volatility is permanently absent because no exchange lists an SGD FX option, so there is no ATM level, no percentile, no term structure, no risk reversal and no variance risk premium for this pair at any tenor. The only quantitative volatility fact available is realised: payload 20-day at 7.43%, 60-day at 6.99%. That combination — a managed base leg paired with a free-floating quote leg — means the pair's central outcomes are compressed while its tails are inherited entirely from the yen.
expression_assessment.directional_expression: Spot or two-leg synthetic only. With no listed option on the cross and no forward funding differential quotable from the payload, the view cannot be expressed with convexity in the pair itself. Against that, the growth differential is enormous and unambiguous: plus 5.9 per cent year on year against roughly plus 0.55 per cent, a forecast lifted to 4.5 to 5.5 per cent, unemployment 2.0 against 2.4 per cent. The reinforcing bullish cluster is unusually coherent for a cross: strong growth, a terms-of-trade shock that costs the quote currency ten per cent of its traded basket against under one per cent for the base, a sovereign differential of Aaa against A1 that is actively repricing with the ten-year JGB at 3.00 per cent for the first time since 1996, and a risk regime — VIX at 14.4, high yield at 260 basis points, both equity indices near records — in which the yen's haven bid is dormant and its funding role is active. The conflicting cluster is smaller but heavier where it counts: a compressing rate differential with three scheduled Bank of Japan decisions to deliver it, and an event-risk asymmetry that is genuinely bilateral and rarely seen — Japan has spent roughly JPY 27.1 trillion buying yen this year with the US Treasury publicly committed to joining again, while MAS has stated it stands ready to curb excessive volatility in the S$NEER. Both official sectors lean against this pair rising and neither leans against it falling. On what is priced versus what we expect: the September hike is in the price, so the tactical repricing risk is the pace language rather than the decision, and the offsetting unpriced item is a 55 per cent probability of an October MAS steepening against published calls nearer 35 to 40 per cent. The path of least resistance while the carry regime holds and the growth gap stays at 535 basis points is a grind higher, contested around 17 to 18 September. The dated catalysts, in order of importance, are the Bank of Japan on 18 September, Japan's national CPI on 17 September, the FOMC on 16 September and Singapore's August CPI on 23 September. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the score is carried by breadth against a bearish heavyweight, because no options market exists in which to buy convexity for either direction, and because the two theses in the underlying dossiers are both credible and mutually cancelling.

strategic.score_interpretation: Applied weights sum to exactly 1.00 and the contributions sum to +0.0416, which is Neutral under the mechanical rule and is the correct answer for a cross where both legs are independently bullish. Three positives total +0.2284 — External Balance +0.1054, Fiscal +0.0680 and Inflation and Growth +0.0550 — against three negatives totalling -0.1868, of which Policy and Rates is -0.1320. The single largest factor and the single largest positive nearly cancel outright: the quote currency's rate advantage arrives at almost exactly the pace at which its terms of trade and sovereign arithmetic deteriorate. Four factors score exactly zero at a combined weight of 0.28, including Guidance at 0.12, where two hawkish and equally under-priced central banks genuinely offset. This is not a thin Neutral produced by weak evidence; it is a Neutral produced by two well-identified blocs of roughly equal force, which is why conviction is 2 rather than 1.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the pair becomes a contest between the quote currency's rate path and the quote currency's balance sheet, and they very nearly cancel. Policy and Rates at 0.24 is the heaviest factor and it is negative because the Bank of Japan's terminal is now put at 1.75 per cent by half of 36 surveyed economists, with 35 of 54 expecting at least 1.50 per cent by end-March 2027 — a level that crosses above Singapore's overnight money-market rate of 1.4028 per cent and flips the bilateral carry from plus 40 basis points to negative, something MAS cannot answer because its instrument delivers only 60 to 75 basis points of trade-weighted appreciation over six months across a basket in which the yen is a minority weight. Against that stand two positives of almost equal combined force. External Balance at 0.17 is the heaviest positive contributor: Japan's terms of trade have fallen from 90.5 in the first quarter to 81.62 in July, a 9.8 per cent transfer of real income abroad, its goods account has turned to deficit with mineral fuels at 22.1 per cent of imports and up 53.5 per cent year on year on falling volumes, and its record headline current-account surplus is 27.6 times more primary income than goods, which generates far less spot demand than Singapore's 16.7 per cent-of-GDP surplus recycled through reserve accumulation and an institutionally appreciating band. Fiscal at 0.10 is the second: every 100 basis points of Bank of Japan tightening adds roughly JPY 5 trillion to a debt-service line already at a record JPY 36.6 trillion on an assumed rate raised to 3.8 per cent, while the Bank cuts its own JGB purchases from JPY 2.5 trillion a month to JPY 2.1 trillion by the first quarter of 2027 — which is precisely why the yen failed to rally through a ten-year yield at 3.00 per cent, and why a risk-premium-driven yield rise is pair-positive rather than pair-negative. The two dossiers' standalone views are therefore not merely reinforcing or conflicting; they are describing the same tightening cycle from opposite sides, and the bilateral question is whether the yen's rate advantage or its fiscal cost arrives first. What is priced against what we expect is again the decisive question, and here the answer is uncomfortable: no bank publishes an SGD/JPY forecast, but crossing the published leg consensus — a 23-desk USD/JPY mean of 154.22 for December against MUFG's USD/SGD of 1.2900 — implies a market expecting this cross lower, while crossing the two dossiers' own central expectations implies it higher, so consensus in this pair is genuinely undefined rather than merely disagreed with. The path of least resistance is a range in which the base currency's growth and balance-sheet advantage is repeatedly offset by dated yen repricing, with no directional progress the score can justify. The catalysts that would break it are the 30 October Bank of Japan Outlook Report, the 10 November tariff-truce expiry, the 18 December decision and the FY2027 draft budget in late December. Conviction is 2 rather than 1 because the offsetting blocs are large, specific and dated rather than vague, and because a Neutral built from two identified mechanisms is more useful downstream than a Neutral built from an absence of evidence.

First, External Balance: consensus treats Japan's record headline current-account surplus as structural currency support without decomposing it, when primary income is 27.6 times the goods surplus and it is the goods account — now in deficit and 4.1 times wider year on year — that generates spot flow, while Singapore's 16.7 per cent-of-GDP surplus is recycled through reserve accumulation and an institutionally appreciating band. Where we agree with consensus is on the rate path itself, which is why the strategic stance is Neutral rather than Bullish.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the Bank of Japan's tightening cycle keeps generating its own fiscal risk premium while Japan's energy import bill and goods deficit persist, the yen fails to convert a compressing differential into currency strength — as it has repeatedly this year through a record joint intervention, a 30-year high in JGB yields and a narrowing UST-JGB spread — and the base currency's growth, external and sovereign advantages assert themselves in the cross rather than only in the trade-weighted index.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The stances differ because two weights move in opposite directions between horizons while the underlying facts stay the same. Inflation and Growth carries 0.18 tactically against 0.10 strategically, so the 535 basis point growth gap contributes +0.1044 over four weeks and only +0.0550 over six months; Flows and Positioning turns from Neutral to Bearish as the insurer hedge-ratio channel becomes relevant; and Policy and Rates, negative on both horizons, gains force as the Bank of Japan's terminal crosses above Singapore's money-market rate. The bullish factors that survive the transition — External Balance and Fiscal, which together rise from a combined 0.14 to 0.27 of weight — grow enough to hold the score near zero but not enough to keep it above the threshold. The thesis therefore weakens with time rather than reversing, which is the correct configuration for a cross whose base currency appreciates mechanically but slowly and whose quote currency reprices in dated steps.

The 30 October round is where the quote currency's terminal is most likely to be marked higher; the December budget is where the fiscal offset that has so far neutralised that repricing either holds near the stated JPY 40 trillion issuance cap or breaks. Hold the strategic view as a range framework between 121.00 and 126.00 rather than as a position.

A weak tail would confirm the fiscal-premium channel and be pair-positive despite higher Japanese yields, which inverts the naive differential read; a strong auction lets the policy channel dominate and is pair-negative.

catalysts.event: Japan August merchandise trade statistics and 8 September balance of payments
catalysts.rationale: The direct measure of the pair's largest strategic positive. July showed a JPY 638.3 billion trade deficit, 4.1 times wider year on year, with mineral fuels at 22.1 per cent of imports and up 53.5 per cent on falling volumes, and June produced Japan's first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months. A second consecutive current-account deficit would be the first back-to-back pair since 2022 and would confirm that the quote currency's headline surplus is no longer generating spot demand.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A 25 basis point hike is carried at 57 to 68 per cent depending on source. The transmission to this cross is second-order and asymmetric rather than absent: a hawkish Fed lifts both dollar legs but the yen is the high-beta funding currency while the Singapore dollar is managed against a basket, so it typically weighs harder on the quote leg and supports the pair. A hold would be the larger surprise and would compress the yen's funding disadvantage, which is pair-negative.

July printed 1.9 per cent headline and 1.8 per cent core against a Bank of Japan ex-special-factors measure of 2.3 per cent, with government energy subsidies suppressing the headline by roughly 40 to 50 basis points and the Board having already guided that core moves clearly above 2 per cent from the second half of fiscal 2026. Tokyo core has accelerated three months running. An upside print hardens the September hike and the pace language, compressing the pair's remaining 40 basis point carry advantage.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The largest single dated event in the tactical window and the only scheduled policy decision for either currency inside it, per the gated calendar. A 25 basis point hike to 1.25 per cent is carried at roughly 80 to 90 per cent and would cut the bilateral money-market advantage from 40.3 to about 15 basis points. Because the decision is largely priced, the pair-relevant risk is the press conference: a repetition of the Summary of Opinions formulation about a pace faster than market expectations would pull December pricing forward and hit the cross harder than the hike itself.

catalysts.event: Singapore August CPI and MAS Consumer Price Developments
catalysts.rationale: The base currency's only data event of consequence in the tactical window and the mechanism by which the market's roughly 35 to 40 per cent probability of an October band steepening converges on the base dossier's 55 per cent. July core rose to 2.0 per cent on an 8.7 per cent jump in electricity and gas as the third-quarter tariff passed through; August carries a full month of that pass-through. A core print at or above 2.2 per cent makes a steepening the base case and is directly pair-positive because in Singapore the exchange rate is the instrument.

Where the base currency's growth advantage is most at risk. Semiconductor output growth has fallen from plus 37.0 per cent in May to plus 20.8 per cent in June to plus 8.0 per cent in July, and total electronics output from plus 35.8 to plus 11.2 per cent over the same three months. A further leg toward zero would undercut the 4.5 to 5.5 per cent growth forecast that carries Factor 2 and the October steepening case, narrowing the 535 basis point growth differential that is the pair's largest tactical positive.

catalysts.event: US FY2027 appropriations deadline and Japanese interim fiscal half-year end
catalysts.rationale: Two coincident events that both favour the quote currency. A US shutdown is precedented — two occurred already in 2026 — and would be risk-negative, which lifts the yen more than the Singapore dollar because the yen's haven bid is global while Singapore's is regional. Separately the Japanese interim book close generates documented repatriation and dividend-related yen demand, and insurer hedge ratios at record lows mean an unusually high share of that flow hits spot rather than rolling off existing forwards.

catalysts.event: MAS October Monetary Policy Statement, Macroeconomic Review and Q3 advance GDP estimate
catalysts.rationale: The densest information event in the Singapore calendar, with all three releases landing together, and the base dossier puts 55 per cent on a further slight steepening of the S$NEER slope toward roughly 1.50 per cent a year against Goldman Sachs expecting no change and CIMB expecting plus 25 basis points. A steepening raises the mechanical appreciation rate of the trade-weighted index and is pair-positive; a hold unwinds an estimated 1.7 per cent band deviation toward midpoint, and unwinds are faster than grinds. No SGD schedule exists on the gated central-bank calendar file, so this date is carried from the base dossier as best available and flagged, not as gated.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: The gated calendar marks this as a projection round, which moves a yen cross materially harder than a bare statement. The July Outlook already revised FY2027 core CPI up to 2.4 per cent and described price risks as skewed to the upside; an October revision incorporating the terms-of-trade shock and the subsidy unwind is the most likely single occasion for the market to mark the Bank of Japan's terminal above 1.75 per cent, which is the level at which the pair's bilateral carry turns negative.

A double hit to the pair. Singapore sends 22.0 per cent of its goods exports to Greater China against Japan's 17.5 per cent to China and is the most trade-dependent large economy in the set, so a lapse damages the base economy's entrepot function at both ends; simultaneously the risk-off it would produce is the environment in which the yen is bought as the funding currency unwinds. Reciprocal Chinese truce expiry follows on 19 November and the exclusion process on 31 December.

Acute for both legs but more so for the base currency, whose export boom is now concentrated in integrated circuits and disk media with Taiwan among its largest destinations, and whose semiconductor output growth has already fallen from plus 37.0 per cent in May to plus 8.0 per cent in July. Any Taiwan-related market disruption transmits to Singapore through the electronics channel while transmitting to the yen through the haven channel, so the two effects compound against the pair.

The date coincides with year-end balance-sheet compression in the Asian dollar market where Singapore is a major clearing centre, and it arrives with Federal Reserve reserve balances draining at roughly USD 20 billion a week. A funding squeeze is the single most reliable mechanism for a sharp fall in this cross: it forces a carry unwind that buys the quote currency while tightening dollar conditions for the base currency's banking system.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The gated calendar's final JPY decision in the window and the largest identified gap between guidance and pricing in either dossier: cumulative pricing implies only about 1.21 per cent after this meeting, i.e. one hike and essentially nothing more in 2026, against a Board writing that the pace will be faster than market expectations and a consensus terminal of 1.75 per cent. A December move would take the yen's policy rate to 1.50 per cent, above Singapore's overnight money-market rate, flipping the pair's carry negative.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 draft budget Cabinet approval
catalysts.rationale: The specific event that decides whether the fiscal channel or the policy channel dominates the yen into 2027. Ministry requests total about JPY 143 trillion with a record JPY 36.6 trillion debt-service line struck at a 3.8 per cent assumed rate, against a Prime Minister aiming to cap new issuance near JPY 40 trillion versus JPY 29.6 trillion in the FY2026 initial budget. A breach of that cap widens the fiscal risk premium and is pair-positive, because it neutralises the yen's rate advantage. Date inferred from the FY2026 precedent of 26 December 2025; the exact Cabinet date is not published and is flagged.

assumptions: Price series actually delivered: the price payload provided 130 weekday bars covering 2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03, with spot 122.96204 at spotDate 2026-09-03. Moving averages, zones, 52-week figures and the 200-week average are computed over the whole stored history — 2007-12-24 to 2026-09-03, 4,879 weekday bars — not just the 130 bars shown. Pip size is 0.01. The payload's dataQuality array flags only 1 resistance / 10 support zones met the two-touch threshold, and 130 daily bars passed downstream (2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03), the 1-6 month strategic horizon. weekendBarsDropped is 0, so every window is a true trading-day window.

spotDate postdates the valuation date by two sessions: VALUATION_DATE is 2026-09-01; the payload spot is the 2026-09-03 close. Every level, target, stop, pip figure, percentage and distance-to-average in this report is anchored to 122.96204, and no fresher web quote has been substituted anywhere.

The pass-1 'spot discrepancy' is resolved and was a date mismatch, not a data conflict: the payload's 31 August close (125.66875) matches the base dossier's SGD/JPY figure to five decimal places, and its 28 August close (125.59609) matches the quote dossier's 125.596. The 287-pip difference is simply the pair falling from 125.83134 on 1 September to 122.96204 on 3 September as the yen rallied on intervention speculation and Bank of Japan repricing.

Moving-average basis: all averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. The 200-week average at 112.67962 is treated as a first-class structural level, converging on spot from beneath at roughly 6.7 yen a year (approximately 79 weeks away), which is structurally supportive but outside this horizon.

Two figures in the carried-verbatim Factor 9 text are superseded by the payload and are flagged rather than corrected: 20-day realised volatility of 3.92% and 60-day of 6.05% from the quote dossier's cross table versus the payload's 7.43% and 6.99%, and the 'lowest 20-day realised volatility of any yen cross' characterisation no longer holds on payload figures. Factor stances, confidences, evidence types and weights are carried unchanged per protocol.

Structural absences, not research gaps: implied volatility does not exist for this pair at any tenor because no exchange lists an SGD FX option; the funding block is unavailable because SGD has no listed future on CME or Eurex and no SGD/JPY cross-currency basis is published by any free venue. The Forward vs Spot section presents an indicative covered-interest-parity derivation from the money-market spread, explicitly labelled, omitting term premium and cross-currency basis.

Singapore has no policy interest rate: MAS's instrument is the slope, width and centre of the S$NEER band. Every bilateral rate figure in this report is a money-market spread using SORA at 1.4028% (2026-08-31) as an explicitly labelled proxy. The S$NEER slope of about 1.25% a year and the band deviation of roughly 1.7% above midpoint are analyst reconstructions whose publisher pages returned empty bodies on re-verification; they are best available and flagged.

Vintage inconsistency in sovereign yields is labelled at every occurrence: the payload's JPY ten-year of 2.67% is a monthly series as of 2026-06-01 and is never quoted as a live level; the 2.943% JGB and 2.42% SGS figures used for the current ten-year differential come from the two dossiers for 31 August, with the SGS leg resting on a single source flagged as best available.

Zone shortfall and how it was supplemented: the payload cleared only one resistance zone against ten support zones at the two-touch threshold. Resistance was supplemented with round numbers (124.00, 125.00, 126.00), the moving-average cluster, and swing structure drawn from the 130 delivered bars, clearly labelled as supplements rather than computed zones.

Weight adjustments: Factor 5 +0.02/+0.01 on the order-of-magnitude bilateral energy asymmetry; Factor 8 +0.02/+0.03 on an actively repricing sovereign differential with a dated crystallising event; Factor 10 -0.04/-0.04 for a non-USD cross, within the framework's contemplated 0.03-0.05 range. Both horizons sum to exactly 1.00.
Net stance derivation follows mechanically from the score: +0.1228 is at or beyond +0.10 and is therefore Bullish; +0.0416 lies between the thresholds and is therefore Neutral.

Where this report disagrees with the settled direction: the tactical Bullish verdict was scored without the price payload. The fundamentals underlying that score — growth gap, terms-of-trade asymmetry, sovereign differential — are intact, but the timing is poor: the two dated risks pass 1 named (Factor 1's BoJ repricing and Factor 7's official-flow asymmetry) both fired on 2-3 September, taking 287 pips out of the pair and turning its swing structure to lower highs and lower lows. The Bullish tactical stance should be read as a conditional entry instruction rather than a position.

Bilateral trade: the IMF DOTS block contains a mirror asymmetry disclosed rather than averaged — Singapore reports exports to Japan of USD 17.8bn and imports of USD 22.2bn, while Japan reports exports to Singapore of USD 19.8bn and imports of USD 7.6bn. The stated net of -USD 4.5bn for the base currency uses the Singapore-reported legs.

Consensus construction and what was excluded: no bank research house publishes an SGD/JPY forecast, so the consensus discussion crosses individually corroborated leg forecasts and labels the construction. Aggregator price-prediction sites (CoinCodex, LongForecast, 30rates, gov.capital, audtoday) are algorithmic extrapolations rather than research and are not relied upon; an article attributing 2026 SGD/JPY ranges of 113.00-118.20 to named banks is flagged as stale and not relied upon.

Bilateral investment flows: targeted searching produced only descriptive, undated or non-quantified material on Japan-Singapore cross-holdings; no bilateral portfolio-flow series was obtainable, so the channel is documented as a gap rather than proxied.
